facts.text: An equivalence argument, also called a similarity argument, is a reasoned and evidenced claim that evidence gathered on one machine variant holds for another because their differences do not affect safety-relevant behavior.
facts.quote: An equivalence argument, also called a similarity argument, is the reasoned and evidenced claim that evidence gathered on one machine variant also holds for another, because the differences between them do not affect the safety-relevant behavior.

facts.text: The booklet recommends a parameterized machine-family model rather than twenty unrelated models, covering geometry and articulation, mass and payload, braking dynamics, grade capability, sensor type and firmware, mounting height and angle, occlusion, vibration, sensor-to-brake latency, and environment.
facts.quote: with parameters for geometry and articulation, mass and payload, braking dynamics, grade capability, sensor type and firmware, mounting height, angle and occlusion, vibration, sensor-to-brake latency and the environment [Chapter 10]

facts.text: For every transition between machine variants, the safety case should record what changed as a configuration-controlled delta.
facts.quote: For every transition from machine A to machine B the safety case answers three questions. What changed, recorded as a configuration-controlled delta?

facts.text: For every transition between machine variants, the safety case should use sensitivity analysis to show whether the change can affect a validated phenomenon or safety output.
facts.quote: Can that change affect a validated phenomenon or safety output, shown by sensitivity analysis?

facts.text: Bridging evidence for machine-variant transfer should comprise no additional evidence for irrelevant differences, targeted tests for influential differences, and new full-system anchors where new physics appears.
facts.quote: What bridging evidence closes the gap: none for irrelevant differences, targeted tests for influential ones, new full-system anchors where new physics appears?

facts.text: A machine-family model is validated at envelope corners: the smallest and largest machine, lowest and highest sensor mount, lightest and heaviest mass, and least and most favorable brake response.
facts.quote: The model is validated at the corners of the envelope (smallest and largest machine, lowest and highest mount, lightest and heaviest mass, least and most favorable brake response)

facts.text: A new machine variant is shown to lie inside the validated machine-family hull and then receives a reduced physical "delta" test set, typically brake calibration plus sensor field-of-view and detection checks at the new mount.
facts.quote: a new variant is shown to lie inside that hull and then gets a reduced "delta" physical set, typically a brake calibration plus a sensor field-of-view and detection check at the new mount.

facts.text: Because geometry, articulation and brake dynamics can act non-monotonically, a machine-variant equivalence argument must demonstrate that the extreme variants bound intermediate variants.
facts.quote: Because geometry, articulation and brake dynamics can act non-monotonically, the claim that the extremes bound the middle must itself be demonstrated [Chapter 10].

facts.text: Moving a sensor can invalidate the validated simulation envelope even when the software is unchanged.
facts.quote: moving a sensor can invalidate the validated simulation envelope even with the software unchanged [Chapter 3]

facts.text: The machine with the worst stopping distance is not necessarily the machine with the worst sensor occlusion, so variant-transfer validation may need several representative machines.
facts.quote: the machine with the worst stopping distance is not necessarily the one with the worst sensor occlusion, so several representatives may be needed [Chapter 1]

facts.text: The booklet found no published off-road example of machine-variant transfer.
facts.quote: no published off-road example of variant transfer was found [Chapter 10].

facts.text: Whether the product range can collapse into a few validated parameterized machine families is a key experiment, not an established fact; both the program schedule and business case depend on the answer.
facts.quote: Whether the product range collapses into a few validated parameterized families is "a key experiment, not a fact", and both the schedule and the business case depend on the answer [Chapter 13].
